Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

New holiday data counts ads inside Google AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT across five shopping categories and shows which prompts ChatGPT ads ran on.

Adthena reported that approximately 175,100 paid ad placements were found within Google’s AI Overview panel as well as AI Mode panels inside the U.S. during the period of June to September. This included five holiday shopping categories; however, the majority of these paid placements belonged to apparel and consumer electronics.

The Holiday AI Paid Search Report also counts 204,489 ChatGPT ad placements in the same five categories over the same months. Adthena sells ad tracking for Google and ChatGPT, and the report closes with an offer for a free trial of its ChatGPT Ads product.

Some U.S. apparel and electronics advertisers may already be using portions of their existing campaigns to serve ads to users who see AI Overviews and AI Mode. The report identifies where the ads appeared, but does not track which ads were clicked, how much was spent, nor what conversions were achieved on either surface.

The total number of ads in Google’s AI Answers (in the U.S.) in this report is based upon a combined total for both AI Overviews and AI Mode. In that count, apparel has approximately 111,000 placements; consumer electronics have about 55,000; travel has roughly 6,500; beauty has about 2,100; and toys and games have around 685.

There are no separate ad buys for these placement types. According to Google’s Help Page regarding Ads in AI-Powered Experiences, all Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns that exist are automatically eligible to appear in AI-Answers. Although advertisers cannot specifically target only AI Overviews or AI Mode, or opt out of those placements apart from Search, they may still utilize negative keyword targeting and/or brand exclusions.

The report also reviewed how many times AI Overviews appeared in Google Results for both August of 2025 and August of 2026. Going from 304 million to 575 million, U.S. appearances saw an 89% increase over that period. The UK/EU saw an increase of 160%, while Australia saw an increase of 536%. The report doesn’t describe the queries behind those counts or say whether the set stayed the same across both years.

The report counts 204,489 ChatGPT Ads placements across five categories, Apparel, Consumer Electronics, Travel, Toys & Games and Beauty, from June through September 2026.

Adthena’s press release frames it more broadly, stating more than 200,000 advertisement placements occurred since OpenAI started allowing others to buy advertising space on the chatbot.

In the report’s count, apparel accounted for the largest number of advertisement placements at 90,517. Next was Consumer Electronics with 56,569; then Travel with 48,134; followed by Toys and Games with 4,694 and lastly Beauty with 4,575.

In addition, the company reported that there were 1,082 different advertisers in those five categories using the service in June, 3,741 advertisers in July, and 6,333 advertisers in August. The company projected the number of advertisers in September.

According to the report, the advertisers in its data in Toys and Games increased the most during that time frame from June to August, increasing 13 fold, from what the company calls a relatively low base.

The report states that the total number of advertiser placements included in their research covered all markets, but does not identify which markets or state whether they continued to monitor the same market(s)/queries throughout the entire four-month period. In addition, OpenAI expanded its footprint during that time.

On August 18, OpenAI announced that ChatGPT Ads would be available in 31 European countries. The company began offering this service one week later. Additionally, on September 23, OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Ads to seven additional Asian markets.

For perspective, on October 21 OpenAI stated that more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT Ads since the advertising capability was opened up to outside parties just over eight months earlier. This figure represents all categories and the complete period of time that ChatGPT Ads has been open to third-party advertisers, so it isn’t directly comparable to the report’s monthly counts.

In addition to that, the report groups ChatGPT ads based on the nature of the search that an ad was run against. It describes research and discovery queries as “people comparing or asking what’s best rather than naming a product.”

In beauty, 83% of ads ran on those queries, while travel and toys & games were at 69% and 67% respectively. Apparel and consumer electronics came in under half, at 48% and 42% respectively.

Again, the press release references only the data related to beauty, travel and toys. The report provides no information about how questions were categorized.

Since Google includes searches that prompt ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode in aggregate in its standard reports for all of Search, they are intermingled throughout your search terms report.

In ChatGPT, best-of and comparison prompts carried most of the observed ads in beauty, travel & toys, and less than 50% of those seen in apparel and electronics.

After the report’s time frame closed, Google’s ads within their AI answers continued to evolve. Google announced that they were launching multi-turn ads in the United States on October 28. These allow advertisers’ ads to show up on subsequent searches (queries) in AI Mode. In addition, Google stated that ads in AI Mode are scaling to ten additional countries including Canada and Australia. They further stated that Brazil, Mexico and the United Kingdom were planned for Q4 2026.

OpenAI’s October 21 announcement expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries. The most recent Adthena data is from September so does not include these new developments nor the weeks surrounding Black Friday.

#7512. How Fresh Step used AI to go from brief to ads at one-tenth the cost

The Clorox cat litter brand worked with agency RECE to get a new campaign in market in about a month.

Since its launch in 1984, Fresh Step has been the crown jewel of Clorox’s cat litter portfolio, a segment of the CPG marketer’s business that has lagged for some time and does not command the share of the $5 billion U.S. cat litter market that executives would like. The company determined that part of the brand’s problem was heightened category pressure on its core promise around odor control.

“Perceptions of [Fresh Step] had actually started to dip. Not core perceptions — it was still good — but relative perceptions,” Eric Schwartz, CMO of The Clorox Company, said about Fresh Step during a presentation at the Association of National Advertisers Masters of Marketing conference last month.

To address those issues and reassert Fresh Step’s positioning as being superior in odor control, the brand needed a new campaign that would be memorable and engaging, but made quickly. The marketer wanted to be able to pivot easily, if needed, rather than be stuck after betting the farm on a creative concept.

“There's a real business pressure, and it was not going to be acceptable [to say] I'll come in six months with my idea,” Deb Crandall, senior marketing director on litter at The Clorox Company, said in an interview. “We need things in market ASAP.”

Fresh Step teamed with artificial intelligence-powered agency RECE — short for radical empathy and creative excellence — to go from brief to finished ad creative on three 15-second spots in 30 days and at one-tenth the cost of a traditional production (and without having to rely on finicky cat actors).

“The speed AI creates lets us bring strategy, concept, copy, direction, AI artists, editors and composers together, all at once. It’s closer to a tech startup’s prototyping process than a traditional ad agency’s,” Toygar Bazarkaya, founder and chief creative officer at RECE, said in emailed comments.

The ads are rolling out now across linear TV with cutdowns on social and will be live by Nov. 9.

“This campaign could not have existed in this way, probably even a year ago. That's how fast I think the advances [in AI] are coming,” Crandall said. “The technology unlocked some magic that wouldn't have been possible without it.”

Fresh Step’s new ads feature a cast of talking cats of different breeds with different accents and attitudes. The spots deliver the brand’s value proposition around odor in different ways: a dog can no longer smell its way to a litter box; a huge cat is no problem for the brand; and cats line up around the block to use Fresh Step.

The brief began as usual, with a business challenge and a consumer insight. AI helped to rapidly prototype creative concepts to show what was resonating, delivering emotion in a way that a script on the page can’t always do. Being able to see talking cats in action helped convince the brand that the ads would still connect with consumers.

“One of the fears was would AI cats give you that same emotive response as when you see a real animal? I think the work does deliver on that. It captures that emotional response,” Crandall said. “That inner part of the process — being able to see it and feel it like midstream — really helped us to unlock and push us into some new spaces that we hadn't been before as a brand.”

The fact that AI-powered content creation technology is trained on an internet that is still overloaded with cat videos may make it easier for the AI-created talking cats to cross the uncanny valley than AI-created humans. And while consumers are wary of AI in ads, the Fresh Step ads are clearly computer generated.

“As consumers, we're all experimenting with this technology in our lives and figuring out how it helps us and doesn't help us,” Crandall said. “This, to me, was very clearly AI. We're not trying to fool anybody here. We're using it to dramatize situations that many cat owners can relate to.”

The speed and cost efficiency of the AI-created campaign will help Fresh Step reinvest in the brand: Getting it done at one-tenth the cost roughly equates to being able to create 10 more campaigns.

“It's always a sign when you've hooked onto something when you can already think of the next five ideas that you want to go do. We have some other things that we're thinking about creating once we get these out there and see how they resonate,” Crandall said. “It's that beautiful blend of humor and connecting to real cat-parent truths that I think is the secret sauce.”

Plus, the creativity unlocked by technology is helping the brand to extend the campaign into what CMO Schwartz referred to as systems of relevance that continuously deliver organic content.

“The deliberately modular design lets us adapt benefits, innovations, packaging, even messages based on what we will learn about consumers in market,” the executive said of the campaign at the ANA event. “That's the real advantage. This isn't a piece of creative we had to bet big on, and now we let it fly and leave it alone. We can keep learning, refining and improving as we go.”

#7511. Reddit tests ads in search results

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform wants to help advertisers align their promotions with users’ discovery behavior even as the company’s overall search traffic drops.

Reddit is testing ads in search results in the app, as the platform looks for more ways to help advertisers align with discovery behaviors.

As shown in these example screens, Reddit’s search ads will be targeted by query, and will include a small ad marker in the upper section of the panel.

As explained by Reddit: “People come to Reddit seeking human perspectives and experiences they can’t find elsewhere, with half of Reddit users saying the platform helps them discover something new. As we continue improving the user search experience on Reddit, we’re also beginning to test ad placements in search. These placements leverage existing ad targeting in search results pages on Reddit, which have high purchase and search intent.”

Reddit said the promotions will be shown in search results based on a range of factors, though these will primarily be aligned with contextual relevance.

Reddit has been working to improve its discovery tools as the app tries to help users find more relevant matches for their queries.

In July, Reddit published a study that found that 72% of its users come to the platform seeking information, and 64% of them have a specific goal in mind.

That also aligns with how Reddit gains traffic from search results, since the platform gets significant citation volume from AI chatbots.

However, AI traffic has started to dry up. Last week, as part of its Q3 performance update, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said that the company’s search traffic dropped by more than 1 million referrals per week on average in October.

That could reduce the value of its own in-app discovery process, though Tuesday’s announcement suggests that Reddit is clearly hoping to maintain its value as a product discovery tool.

Reddit said that it will initially test ads in search with a select group of eligible advertisers.

#7509. November Click Spikes In Google Search Console Are Bot Traffic – How To Filter Your Reports via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

That sudden click spike in Search Console isn’t real traffic. Here’s what my data shows, what’s causing it, and how to filter it out.

Earlier this week, I saw Barry Schwartz’s post on X (and his write-up on Search Engine Roundtable) sharing a screenshot from Joy Hawkins. Joy noticed that several sites were seeing sudden, massive vertical spikes in Google Search Console clicks while impressions stayed flat, and Barry asked a great follow-up question: “Anyone else seeing this? If so, how are you filtering the report…”

Screenshot of Barry Schwartz and Joy Hawkins’ post on X highlighting the sudden click spike in Google Search Console. (Image Credit: Marie Haynes)

When I saw Barry’s tweet, I immediately thought this would be the ultimate real-world test for Marie’s Brain – my soon-to-be-launched agentic SEO and AI search analysis system.

Over the past several months, I have been building Marie’s Brain to combine my 15+ years of research on Google’s ranking systems with live, programmatic access to the Search Console and analytics data of the sites I monitor. Instead of manually clicking through Search Console property by property to see if any of my clients were affected, I asked my system to scan across all of the sites I monitor, check the unfinalized fresh data through Nov. 2, 2026, and flag any property showing a sudden anomaly in clicks.

Within seconds, Marie’s Brain surfaced the exact same vertical spike across multiple sites in completely different industries – and pulled the raw page, query, device, and country dimensions so I could see what was actually happening under the hood.

Just like Glenn Gabe and Joy Hawkins mentioned in Barry’s Search Engine Roundtable post, the majority of properties I monitor showed completely normal traffic. However, while some SEOs saw the wave begin over the weekend (Oct. 31 to Nov. 1), a distinct subset of sites I monitor experienced a dramatic vertical spike on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026 that mirrors Joy’s screenshot:

Six-month daily Google Search Console clicks (Search type: Web, including fresh unfinalized data through Nov. 2, 2026) across three affected properties I monitor. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Here is how those three anonymized properties behaved on Nov. 2, 2026 compared to their prior seven-day baseline (Oct. 26 – Nov. 1, 2026):

When I had my system drill into the raw API rows for Nov. 2, two unmistakable patterns emerged across the affected sites:

Visual summary of why total impressions look flat while automated deep-SERP clicks create a vertical spike in Google Search Console. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Normally, organic clicks in Search Console are heavily concentrated in the top 3 to 5 results on Page 1. On Nov. 2, click-through rate (CTR) exploded on pages ranking between Position 11 and Position 55 (Pages 2 through 6 of Google):

Why did total impressions stay flat if every click also had an impression? It comes down to simple scale. When a site normally gets 18,000 impressions and 50 clicks per day (like Site A), adding 275 automated impressions is only a 1.5% bump on the impression line – completely invisible on a chart! Adding 275 clicks to a 50-click baseline, on the other hand, creates a massive 6.5x vertical spike.

On Site C (a technical troubleshooting Q&A site), a single long-tail troubleshooting page that normally gets zero to one click per day (and never received more than seven clicks in a single day across the entire previous six months) suddenly jumped to 13 clicks on Nov. 1 and 40 clicks on Nov. 2.

While the spikes on Sites A and B came from U.S. searches, all 40 clicks on this Site C page came from Canada. From Oct. 28 to Oct.r 31, that page only had four to seven impressions per day in Canada (and 0 clicks) while ranking on Page 2. Then on Nov. 2, Canadian impressions on that page jumped by ~45 (to 50 impressions), and Canadian clicks jumped from 0 to 40 clicks – meaning almost every single one of those new impressions was clicked (an 80.0% CTR at average position 14.6 on Page 2, while U.S. clicks on that page stayed at 0)!

When I inspected the exact queries that clicked into that single URL on Nov. 2, there were 23 slightly reworded variations of the exact same troubleshooting question (including systematic number permutations like 3 times, 4 times, 5 times, 7 times, 10 times), almost every single one logging 100% CTR (1 click / 1 impression, 2/2, or 3/3) between Position 10.0 and Position 33.0. Other troubleshooting pages on the same site logged 1 click / 1 impression (100% CTR) at Position 45.5 to 54.0.

Normally, when a basic rank tracker or scraper loads a Google search results page, it only generates impressions – not clicks. For Search Console to record a click, a browser or bot has to actually follow (or trigger) Google’s click-tracking link on the search results page.

Looking at the data patterns across these sites, four possibilities stand out:

Because GSC does not let you filter the top performance chart by ranking position or CTR, there is no perfect one-click button to strip only the bot clicks out of your sitewide graph if dozens of pages were affected. However, these three approaches work well depending on how your site was impacted:

If dozens of pages across your whole site spiked on Desktop (like Sites A & B), you cannot exclude every page individually. While filtering the top bar by Device: Mobile obviously hides your legitimate Desktop traffic too, it is a great sanity check to show a client or stakeholder that your Mobile organic trendline is completely normal (on Site A, Mobile clicks were 30 on Nov 2 vs. 27-40 on prior days; on Site B, Mobile clicks were 11 on Nov 2 vs. 11 on Nov 1).

To see the exact pages that were affected on your site:

If you have Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, or an agentic coding environment (like Antigravity or Cursor) connected to the Google Search Console API or a custom MCP server, you can paste this exact prompt to check all of your sites in seconds:

No. Because this is automated activity rather than human visitors, you do not need to change your pages, disavow anything, or panic when those clicks drop right back down to baseline. Just annotate early November 2026 in your reporting (right alongside GSC’s other recent reporting changes) so you and your clients know why Search Console suddenly showed a vertical jump in clicks!

#7508. How marketers can better optimize for AI search visibility

Most of what marketers are expected to spend on artificial intelligence visibility in 2027 is misdirected, writes GeoSurge founder Francisco Vigo.

The following is a guest piece written by Francisco Vigo, co-founder and CEO of AI visibility company GeoSurge. Opinions are the author’s own.

Most of what marketers will spend on artificial intelligence visibility in 2027 is aimed at the wrong end of the process. The standard playbook tunes content for the moment that an assistant searches the web, assuming live search gives every brand a fair shot at being mentioned in AI results. By the time the model searches, though, it has already decided which brands are worth looking up, and it makes that call from memory.

We measured this at GeoSurge. Brands an AI model already remembered were searched about three times as often as brands it didn't, 55.7% versus 17.4%, and for its five most-remembered brands, the rate reached 67%. The pattern held in all nine industries we tested. If memory decides who gets searched, the budget belongs in what builds memory: the coverage, reviews and category association that models learn from between training runs.

When AI assistants first started answering buying questions, brands worried that the model's knowledge was frozen at training time. Live web search seemed to solve that, because whatever the model doesn't know, it can look up in real time. We call that RAG - Retrieval-Augmented Generation. However, before a model can retrieve anything, it has to decide what to search for, and it makes that decision using its own memory, somewhat like a human would.

Modern AI search doesn't run a single query. Ask "what's the best business checking account for a small company" and the model splits it into a batch of parallel searches. Some are generic and some name specific companies. Google calls this “query fan-out.” Every citation and recommendation flows through those queries, and a source that never matches one rarely enters the answer.

To see how memory shapes those queries, we first recorded the brands a model could recall with no web access, across nine industries. Then, over 12 days, we ran 66 realistic buyer questions 60 times each, capturing about 4,000 responses and 13,281 of the searches the model ran behind the scenes. About 69% of those searches were generic category queries. Of the 31% that named a brand, nearly two-thirds named one of the model's top-five remembered brands.

This makes sense mechanically. A model writing search queries draws on the same learned associations it uses to write anything else. It can't search for a brand it never learned, any more than you can Google a restaurant you've never heard of.

The effect isn't uniform, and that matters for marketers who are planning.

For example, in automotive, 82% of brand-specific searches named one of the model's top-five remembered brands; in finance, 77% did. In fitness and wellness, the figure was closer to 50%, because models searched beyond their memory far more often.

Our tentative read, which the study didn't test, is that memory-led categories are dominated by a few long-established, heavily covered brands. Search-led categories, by contrast, have many smaller, newer ones. Each industry rests on six to 12 prompts, so treat the splits as indicative. Still, the distinction is useful. It tells you whether your problem is retrievability, which content and technical work can fix relatively quickly, or memorability, which it can't.

First, diagnose before you spend. In a search-led category, well-structured and highly retrievable content can move results relatively quickly. In a memory-led category, the same work has a much lower ceiling.

Second, fund earned media as infrastructure. Model memory forms from the training corpus: years of press coverage, analyst reports, reviews, forum discussions and consistent association between a brand and its category. These disciplines were long justified in the soft language of “reputation.” Now they have a mechanical function, because they are how a brand gets written into the systems that decide what to search for. They can't be injected at query time; they accrue between training runs, or not at all.

Third, measure recall, not just citations. Counting citations measures the scoreboard, but the game is decided upstream, in what models remember before a single query fires. That scoreboard is also getting cheaper. Tracking that typically costs hundreds of dollars a month now has free options. If seeing the answer costs next to nothing, more of the budget can go toward shaping it.

None of this makes query-time optimization worthless. It works in search-led categories, and even in memory-led ones the generic queries leave room to compete.

But the industry has the priority order backward. The dominant playbook optimizes the last millisecond of a process that is substantially decided months earlier, inside a training run.

For challenger brands, this is urgent. Remembered brands get searched, searched brands get cited and those citations feed the corpus the next generation of models learns from. Each training cycle dominated by incumbents makes that loop harder to break.

You can't win at query time what you lost at training time; however, training time comes around again, and what the models remember next is being written now.

Alphabet’s Q3 numbers show AI Mode growing faster than it earns, and every reason Google gave for the slowdown is temporary except one.

Alphabet just reported the fastest growth in Google search queries in five years; in the same quarter, its search revenue grew at the slowest rate in 2026.

Roger covered the earnings call earlier this week on Search Engine Journal, and it’s a great overview of the high points. I’m diving deeper to make a specific point here.

Search & other revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion in the third quarter, according to Alphabet’s earnings release, down from 19% in the first quarter and 17% in the second. That was roughly $1.6 billion below analyst expectations, and CNBC reported it was the second straight quarter search came in under estimates. On the earnings call, Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, named one of the causes directly: strong growth in AI Mode queries “had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.”

For two years, the argument over whether AI answers cut into search has run on inferred numbers: click-through studies, panel estimates, and referral samples, many from vendors with something to sell. This quarter, the effect shows up in a counted number, Google’s own revenue line, with a Google executive naming AI Mode as a cause. That changes the quality of the evidence, even if it doesn’t finalize the argument.

A quick disclosure before going further: I run a company that measures visibility inside AI answers, so a story about money moving into those answers isn’t neutral ground for me.

The market reaction was severe. Alphabet shares fell about 13% on Thursday, the steepest one-day drop on record, erasing roughly half a trillion dollars in market value. Search wasn’t the only reason. Free cash flow came in at negative $9.07 billion against an expected shortfall of about $2.7 billion, and capital spending is still climbing. So I won’t claim investors sold because they rejected Google’s explanation for search. What I will claim is that the explanation needs a closer read than it’s getting, because the part that matters most is the part Google spent the least time on.

Schindler listed four drivers of the slowdown from the second quarter to the third. Foreign exchange came first, and he called it the single largest driver of the search revenue deceleration. Second, some retail advertisers in Asia-Pacific pulled back after the EU eliminated its de minimis exemption for low-value imports. Third, media and entertainment spending normalized after a second quarter inflated by the FIFA World Cup. Fourth, AI Mode queries grew quickly and earn less than traditional search. CFO Anat Ashkenazi added that Google has started lapping the search acceleration that began in the third quarter of 2025, which makes year-over-year comparisons harder for a few quarters.

Put those drivers on a timeline, and they sort themselves. A currency swing reverses or gets absorbed. The World Cup is over. A trade-rule change gets priced into advertiser budgets within a few quarters. Lapping a strong year is arithmetic that fades on its own. AI Mode is the only factor on the list that gets larger each quarter, because Google is actively growing it, and the lower monetization comes along with every query it adds.

Google’s Q3 explanation for slower search revenue named three temporary factors and one structural one: AI Mode queries are growing faster than they earn, and that gap widens with every quarter of adoption until ad yield inside the answer catches up.

I understand the instinct to dismiss the currency explanation as convenient. I’d rather check it, because Alphabet publishes enough to do that. Total revenue grew 25% in the third quarter whether or not you adjust for currency; the constant-currency reconciliation tables in the release show it, and Ashkenazi described FX as a slight headwind on year-over-year growth. In the second quarter, revenue grew 24%, or 23% in constant currency, which means currency added about a point. Across the whole company, then, currency moved from a slight tailwind to a slight headwind, a swing of a point or two at most.

Ashkenazi also said FX had a more significant impact on a sequential basis, and the release bears that out: Revenue grew 6% from the second quarter as reported and 7% in constant currency. That’s a real effect. It’s also a one-point effect, and it applies to the company as a whole, not to search specifically.

Search growth fell five points over the same period. Google doesn’t publish a constant-currency figure for search alone, so this can’t be determined precisely. But unless search is far more exposed to currency than the rest of Alphabet, my estimate is that FX accounts for something like one to two of those five points. That makes it plausible as the single largest driver, and it still leaves most of the slowdown to the other factors combined.

That distinction matters. “Single largest driver” is a ranking. It tells you FX beat each of the other causes individually. It doesn’t tell you FX explains most of the decline, and it says nothing about which causes will still be there next year. The currency explanation is probably true. It just isn’t the answer to the question investors and practitioners are actually asking, which is whether the new way people search with Google earns as much as the old one.

The other headline number deserves the same scrutiny. Sundar Pichai said Google’s year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it has been in five years. Google didn’t give the rate, and it didn’t say how a query is counted inside an AI Mode session. According to the call transcript, AI Mode queries average three times the length of traditional searches, and Google is now running multi-turn conversations in AI Mode, with ads designed for them. If each turn in a conversation counts as a query, query growth rises mechanically as conversations get longer, whether or not more people are searching for more things.

I’m not claiming that’s how Google counts. I’m saying the record query growth is a counted number with a definition we can’t see, and that kind of number should be held loosely until the definition is published. Revenue is much harder to redefine, which is why the revenue line is where the AI Mode story finally became visible.

In my forecast earlier in October that the SERP stops being Google’s default between 2028 and 2030, I argued the trigger is ad yield. Google flips the default when an answer earns roughly what a results page earns per query, because before that point flipping costs money and after it keeping the old default does. One of the signals I said would push the timeline later was weak returns from AI Mode ad placements.

Q3 is Google confirming, in its own revenue, that parity hasn’t arrived. That fits the forecast’s explanation for why Google isn’t in a hurry to flip anything. It also tells you where Google’s effort goes next. Google isn’t going to slow AI Mode down to protect the results page; Pichai credits AI for the query growth, and the company is plainly committed to it. Instead, Google closes the yield gap by putting more advertising inside the answer.

The call laid that plan out. Schindler said Google is scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries, taking AI Mode ads international for the first time, and introducing multi-turn ads in AI Mode in the U.S. He also said Google’s ad experiments have shown promising results, a phrase that will either become a reported metric in coming quarters or quietly disappear.

None of this surprised me. In August 2025, I described an ad system that builds the ad at query time inside the response, with advertisers supplying inputs rather than finished creative, and placement decided by how closely a brand aligns with the intent behind the prompt. Google shipped an early version at Google Marketing Live in May. Q3 explains why the rest of that design is likely to arrive faster: Google now has a quarterly revenue reason to finish building it.

One line from the call should get more attention from SEOs than it will. Schindler said click-through rates “are already similar between sponsored and organic product list items within AI Mode.” On a traditional results page, organic and paid listings occupied different territory with different click behavior, and practitioners built entire strategies around that separation. Inside an AI Mode answer, by Google’s own account, a sponsored product listing and an organic one draw clicks at about the same rate.

Put that next to the yield gap and my read is straightforward, though I want to be clear it’s my opinion and not something Google said. An answer has a small number of places where a brand can appear. As Google adds ads to close the gap, more of those places become available for purchase, and if sponsored and organic placements perform alike, advertisers have every reason to buy them. Organic visibility inside the answer doesn’t disappear, but it now competes for space with inventory that carries a direct revenue target.

Google also said the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, and that many are upper-funnel queries carrying new commercial intent. That’s Google’s claim, and nobody outside Google can verify it. If it’s accurate, AI Mode is creating commercial moments that never existed on the results page, and the decision about which brands appear in them happens inside the answer, before anyone clicks anything. That’s a strong argument for measuring presence in the answer and not just clicks out of it.

The practical move is to establish a baseline now, before ad load inside AI Mode scales. For the queries that matter most in your category, record which answers cite you, which cite competitors, and which already carry sponsored units alongside the citations. A quarter from now, that record tells you whether paid placements are taking positions organic sources used to hold, and it gives you evidence to bring to budget conversations instead of an impression. Google will report its side of this story in aggregate. Nobody is going to report yours for you.

This is where the difference between counted and inferred numbers stops being academic. Google’s revenue line is counted and audited. The query growth claim is counted but undefined. The incremental-query claim is asserted. Click-through studies of AI answers are inferred from samples. Each deserves a different level of trust, and the mistake I see most often is treating them as interchangeable because they all arrive as percentages. Measuring how brands actually show up inside AI answers, rather than inferring it from traffic, is the problem I built CitationIQ to address, and it becomes harder and more necessary as paid placements fill those answers.

Google’s fourth-quarter report arrives in early February, and Ashkenazi has already said FX will be a slightly larger headwind and lapping will cost a couple of points of growth. Q4 comes with the same cover built in. Here’s what I’ll be looking at instead:

The third-quarter report is the first time the gap between how much people use Google’s AI search and how much it earns appeared in Google’s own revenue, and Google’s response to that gap will be more advertising inside AI answers, where paid and organic placements now compete for the same small set of positions.

This post was originally published on Duane Forrester Decodes.

#7501. Instagram tries to entice long-form creators

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform is using one-off payouts and premium placements to make up for its lack of the type of robust payout system offered by YouTube.

As Instagram makes its new push into long-form content via Features, the platform is also working on other ways to promote long-form video in order to get more people viewing and more creators posting.

A key question from creators, however, has been around monetization, and why they would want to post their longer videos to Instagram, given that its payout system is nowhere near as lucrative as YouTube’s Partner Program.

But even without a solidified payments system in place, Instagram does have some other tricks up its sleeve to get creators sharing more long-form videos.

As shown in these screenshots posted by creator economy expert Lia Haberman, Instagram is highlighting long-form video in a prominent space at the top of its Explore page for some users. That will certainly get the attention of creators, who will see this as a massive opportunity to get more people checking out their content.

Instagram is also reportedly offering one-off payments of up to $500,000 to a selection of big-name creators to get them posting long-form content.

In combination, it seems like Instagram will be able to make Features a bigger consideration for creators, even without a more competitive monetization program.

Though the platform is also working on that element.

Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri has acknowledged the app will have to evolve its payment program to incentivize long-form creators, but it hasn’t worked out the best way to move forward yet.

In an interview with YouTubers Colin and Samir published last week, Mosseri discussed the various challenges Instagram is facing in building a sustainable monetization program.

Mosseri said the aim of adding long-form content on IG was to compete with YouTube, which is now seeing most of its viewership growth via Connected TV, or people watching YouTube videos on their home TV sets. Mosseri said that Instagram, ideally, will be able to integrate short and long-form content into a more Instagram-style approach, where long-form videos can be split into short Reels, thereby providing viewers multiple consumption options.

But on payments, Mosseri said that Instagram was still weighing its options.

Mosseri added that he doesn’t believe platform payments, performance-based incentives or creator bonuses are a revenue driver. Inserting mid-roll ads can also be disruptive, and while Mosseri said Instagram is making one-off payments to bootstrap Features, that isn’t a sustainable path.

Which leaves few options, outside of helping creators organize brand deals to support their content. Mosseri said that Instagram offers certain smaller creator payment schemes, but those have also been historically cost-negative and a losing bet in terms of ROI.

Mosseri’s comments likely won’t give a lot of hope to creators looking to make more money via long-form content in the app. This is especially true given that an external analysis of Instagram’s payout program, conducted by VidIQ, shows that creators on Instagram generally only earn around 10% of what they make on YouTube.

That could eventually see Features going the same way as IGTV, the platform’s previous long-form content play. IGTV also died because there was no financial incentive for creators to post to Instagram instead of posting to YouTube.

Given Mosseri’s comments, it’s hard to see this outcome shifting , even with expanded exposure options.

The FTC unsealed new details in its Amazon Ads lawsuit, alleging hidden surcharges raised CPCs by up to 250% on Prime Day. Here is what advertisers should know.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 22 state attorneys general filed an updated complaint against Amazon with newly unredacted details about how the company allegedly inflated prices in its online search advertising auction.

The FTC and its state partners originally sued Amazon in August in the Western District of Washington, alleging the retailer covertly raised the prices advertisers paid on its platforms.

The newly unsealed material alleges that Amazon secretly increased advertising prices by up to 50% above auction results on ordinary days. During major shopping events like Prime Day and Black Friday, the alleged increases reached 250%.

Read on to learn what the unredacted complaint alleges, how Amazon responded to advertiser questions at the time, and what this means for how you evaluate historical campaign performance.

According to the FTC’s November 5 announcement, the unsealed sections of the complaint outline specific cost-per-click (CPC) increases and revenue targets tied to the alleged surcharges between 2021 and 2023.

The complaint alleges that Amazon’s hidden surcharges affected both small businesses and large advertisers across multiple peak shopping periods:

These examples add detail to the original lawsuit, which challenged how Amazon calculated auction prices and explained those calculations to advertisers.

The unsealed material also links Amazon’s alleged surcharges to internal revenue goals.

According to the complaint, Amazon executives discussed needing an additional $40 million in revenue in 2023 to hit corporate financial targets.

The complaint quotes an email from the head of Amazon Ads to Amazon’s senior vice president of ad products and technology:

I’d like to pull out all of the stops (without doing unnatural acts) to close our gaps to plan. I suspect that the entire gap won’t be closed, so whatever can be done with reserves (ideally at least $40MM would be helpful).

The case concerns Amazon’s use of “soft reserve prices,” which can increase the final CPC above what competing bids would otherwise produce.

A soft reserve differs from a minimum bid required to enter an auction. Amazon says advertisers can win placements below the soft reserve, in which case they pay their bid.

The FTC alleges Amazon used undisclosed reserve pricing to increase advertiser charges while continuing to describe its auctions in misleading terms.

If you managed Amazon Ads between 2021 and 2023, you may remember questioning why CPCs jumped so sharply during peak shopping events.

According to the unredacted complaint, advertisers questioned Amazon directly about whether changes to its auction process explained higher CPCs.

In one instance, an advertiser asked whether “something has changed with respect to the second price auction process, either by design or mistake.”

The FTC alleges that an Amazon account manager gave a misleading response:

After reaching out to the product specialist team we were informed there is not a bug, or a change in auction style, so no worries there. This year the marketplace is even more crowded than any year previous, and we are seeing the spike in CPCs [costs-per-click] as a direct reflection.

The alleged exchange concerns more than whether CPCs increased. It concerns whether Amazon accurately explained the cause when an advertiser asked about changes to the auction.

Campaign reports show what advertisers paid and the performance that followed. They do not reveal how Amazon calculated the final CPC.

In its response to the original lawsuit, Amazon denied deceiving or harming advertisers. The company defended its reserve pricing and said advertisers never pay more than their maximum bid.

While these allegations are still being litigated in federal court, the unsealed details give paid media teams important context for past and current campaign analysis.

If you manage Amazon Ads for your brand or clients, here’s a few proactive steps you can take:

The 2021 through 2023 examples also shouldn’t be read as the full scope of the case. Earlier FTC materials discuss alleged conduct in 2024 and identify Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, and Display Ads.

The FTC’s press release summarizes the newly unredacted allegations, but it doesn’t state whether the alleged surcharge practices continued past 2023 or which specific Amazon search ad formats were included.

The newest release didn’t include a public response from Amazon regarding the newly unsealed details, however, Amazon did provide a full response dispute on August 31st regarding the lawsuit.

We’ll continue to report on this as more information from the court filings becomes available, or if Amazon provides an updated response to this new information.

#7499. Old Navy flies with celebs, Gap keeps it acapella for holiday campaigns

The sister brands are sticking to their respective marketing strengths as the holiday season kicks into high gear.

Old Navy has launched its holiday campaign with a star-studded spot, per details shared with Marketing Dive. Actors Alan Cumming and Meg Stalter serve as flight attendant and pilot, respectively, on the “Jingle Jet,” where passengers include Paris Hilton, Charli D'Amelio, actor True Whitaker and influencer Vidya Gopalan and her family.

The campaign follows the recent launch of a holiday campaign from sister brand Gap that is centered around music. Taken together, these see the brands sticking to their respective marketing strengths as the holiday kicks into high gear.

Old Navy’s campaign was created with the brand’s in-house team and agency BBH USA. It was directed by duo Adam & Dave, with Academy Award-winner Autumn Durald Arkapaw as director of photography. The ad spotlights fashions starting at $7.99 including sequined dresses, matching pajamas and performance fleece and ends with the value-oriented tagline “More Merry For Your Money.”

“At Old Navy, we believe the holidays should be filled with more fun, more style and more possibilities for everyone. From festive fashion to gifts for the whole family, we’re making it easier to celebrate big without compromising,” said Zac Posen, chief creative officer for the brand in press materials.

The campaign is the first effort launched during the tenure of Old Navy CEO Michael Francis, who stepped into the role on Nov. 2, and the latest example of how the retailer has changed its marketing strategy after a recent sales slump.

“Our marketing has been totally rewired … to create more sharper price points and more value orientation with, of course, the Old Navy narrative that keeps our brands really relevant,” Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson said during a Goldman Sachs conference in September.

The Old Navy holiday effort sees the brand re-team with Hilton, who featured in a summer campaign that drove engagement but not traffic, Dickson said at the conference. The brand’s last holiday campaign was in 2024 and starred Jennifer Hudson with a cast of lesser-known characters.

Gap on Nov. 3 rolled out the latest iteration of its “Give Your Gift” campaign, highlighting individuality, creativity and community in an ad that brings together three choirs to sing Jackson 5 classic "I'll Be There.”

“The spirit of this campaign celebrates unity and togetherness. That’s the sentiment we aim to bring to our customers this season, offering new opportunities to engage with our brand and create memorable experiences that bring Gap’s gifting destination to life, both digitally and IRL,” Gap CMO Fabiola Torres said in a statement.

The campaign spans digital, social, video and owned channels and will be extended through immersive shopping experiences, including a multiday pop-up opening in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, this month.

Gap launched the “Give Your Gift” campaign in 2024 with an ad that featured an a cappella version of Janet Jackson’s “Together Again” and returned in 2025 with an ad centered on a cover of Miley Cyrus song “The Climb.”

Gap Inc. comparable sales were down 1% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, with Old Navy down 4% and dragging down overall results at a time when the company's flagship brand Gap saw comp sales increase 10%. The company will release its third quarter earnings on Nov. 19.

#7496. Facebook expands Creator Fast Track program to Brazil

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The program offers incentives for creators not yet posting to Facebook, though the monetary incentives for Brazilian creators are significantly less than what the company offered in North America.

Meta wants to get more creators in Brazil posting to Facebook, so it’s expanding its Creator Fast Track program, which offers guaranteed monthly payments to entice creators who are already popular on other apps to share their content to Facebook as well.

Launched in the U.S. and Canada back in March, the Facebook Creator Fast Track program is aimed at creators who’ve already built an audience elsewhere.

To qualify for Brazil’s version of the program, local creators will need to have at least 20,000 followers on either Instagram, TikTok or YouTube, and have generated at least 30,000 video views over the previous 30 days.

The program is open to creators who haven’t posted a Facebook Reel in the last 6 months and is only valid for “high-quality, original” content.

Those accepted into the program will be required to post at least 20 original Reels on Facebook during each 30-day period over the course of three months. Those Reels need to be posted on separate days, and the videos must be original to Facebook. Creators can re-post content that they’ve shared in other apps, so long as it hasn’t been previously posted on their Facebook Page.

Creators who meet these requirements will be rewarded with guaranteed payments not tied to video performance, but instead linked to audience counts on other apps.

As explained by Meta: “Your monthly payment depends on the highest follower count on one eligible Instagram, TikTok or YouTube account linked during your application. The program uses only your highest follower count from a single account.”

Creators with up to 100,000 followers in one of these apps are eligible to receive $25 per 30-day period, and up to $75 total for the life of the program. Creators with one million followers or more on these other platforms will get $300 per day, up to $900.

Those amounts are significantly lower than what Meta offered creators in the U.S. and Canada in the first iteration of the program.

In the first iteration, creators in the U.S. and Canada with up 100,000 followers were offered up to $450 per month, while those with a million or more followers got $3,000 monthly payments.

It seems that Meta has watered down those amounts for the Brazilian market, which could suggest that the initial scheme didn’t deliver enough return on that outlay to justify the payouts.

Yet, at these lower amounts, it seems unlikely this will be a big lure for creators in Brazil, who, in most cases, are earning significantly more from monetization programs on other apps.

But clearly, Meta is keen to make Facebook more engaging, and by enticing established creators over, it’s hoping that it can then keep them posting to the app by showcasing the value of connecting with the Facebook audience, and tapping into increased video engagement in the app.

As part of its Q1 2026 earnings announcement, Meta reported that total video watch time on Facebook increased by more than 8% globally, representing the largest quarter-over-quarter engagement gain in four years.

#7495. Lenovo NA CMO on telling the ‘full stack story’ through sports

The World Cup drove 4.4 billion social impressions and a 4.2% lift in brand value for the tech company.

Lenovo used its FIFA sponsorship to put its artificial intelligence tools in front of billions of viewers. From the Lenovo AI Referee View to an ad campaign featuring soccer superstar David Beckham, the tech company looked to put itself front-and-center during one of the most watched sports programs in the world. And it worked, earning the brand 4.4 billion social impressions and 1.8 billion creator/influencer impressions, per data provided by the brand.

Over the course of the tournament, Lenovo said it saw a 4.2 times lift in brand consideration among tech-focused soccer fans and a 4.2% lift in brand value. It also claims to have captured the top competitive share of voice among FIFA partners on social media and driven 460,000 page views to Lenovo-owned sites.

Lenovo North America CMO Milo Speranzo sat down with Marketing Dive to talk about making the most of expensive sports sponsorships, how the brand is looking to replicate success with the women’s soccer tournament in 2027 and how it's differentiating itself in the AI race.

The following interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

MILO SPERANZO: Having the same goals, the same messaging and storytelling, as well as the ability for us to integrate our product and technology into the actual event was a key pillar in that decision making of, do we go all in? With FIFA and the World Cup, there's no partial in, or at least doesn't feel like it.

It's an all-in engagement, and when we made that decision in 2024, we were very confident that we had covered all three of our determination silos that we look at in order to really ask ourselves: Will this be a successful partnership? [Those silos are] tech integration, can we tell an authentic story and then the marketing KPIs on the back half. Those three pillars for the World Cup just lined up perfectly.

Yes, it was. When we look at a return on investment for a partnership, the brand piece is a third of what we judge ourselves on. I would say that all of our marketing-specific KPIs were exceeded. It was very much an awareness play, as well as educating our customers that we are not only products. We are a very deeply resourced supply chain-resilient technology solutions company that has a massive AI portfolio.

David is an amazing representative of our brand. He is a wonderful personality for one, but two, he also has an eclectic mix of hobbies. He’s a chicken farmer, small business owner, he builds motorcycles. He embodies what we would consider a potential super-user, and he does use Lenovo. He's very much a brand ambassador of our product line, so when we looked at potential spokespersons for the World Cup, the Beckham-soccer fit was very natural. Lenovo is a global brand. FIFA is a global property, so we did not look at it as a U.S. spokesperson. We looked at it as a global spokesperson.

It's a very different audience. [For the men] we saw massive North America engagement when the North America countries were engaged. We saw engagement stay higher than expectations, drop significantly after the U.S. and Canada were out.

For the women, our U.S. and Canadian teams are just powerhouses. During the men’s tournament, we planned for a lot of our early bespoke, larger events, larger engagements to be really in those early to quarterfinal rounds, and then transitioned to a lot of branding and hospitality as we got into the semis and the finals. For the Women's World Cup, we have to think of it very differently because the eyes of my audience here in North America, I believe, are going to be affixed to this equally across the entire tournament, hopefully all the way into the finals.

For us in North America, the marketing KPIs for the Women's World Cup we feel will exceed what we saw during the men's. That’s for the reasons we just spoke about. Canada and the U.S. women are powerhouses. So, we're really excited to double down in areas that maybe we didn't double down during the men's World Cup.

The men's had more countries, it had more games. There's less [with the Women’s World Cup]. We have a chance to focus our energy, especially our marketing energy, on fewer, bigger campaigns. It'll be everything from bespoke events to hospitality, just being there, to physical sponsorships, to fan fests. There's going to be a couple large fan fests in Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo that we’ll have a pretty big presence at.

As far as differentiation in the tech stack, everybody says they're everything to everybody. In reality, from an ecosystem perspective, Lenovo is the only technology provider that can provide everything from phone to PC to all the adjacencies, the cold screens and mice and portables and battery backups, all the way to the most complex data center solutions.

The answer [to standing out] is storytelling. You'll see a lot of tech companies attach themselves to a brand or a sports brand or a property, but only tell that story as it resonates with the sport. We need to tell that story so it resonates beyond the sports where you're just not getting the value that you should get out of what is a very expensive partnership.

#7493. Snapchat posts modest user increase in Q3

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Company revenue was up, but the platform’s daily active user growth has stalled across nearly every market.

Snap Inc. posted its Q3 2026 earnings report on Wednesday, which showed that user growth on Snapchat has largely stalled, while overall company revenue saw a steady year-over-year increase.

First, on users. Snapchat now has 495 million daily active users, up from 493 million in Q2.

An increase of just 2 million daily actives, quarter over quarter, is not a particularly positive endorsement of the app’s expanded market opportunities. But even more pressing, Snapchat saw no growth at all in daily active users in either the North American or European markets, meaning all user growth came from its Rest of World segment.

This could end up having a broader impact on the platform’s revenue potential, because Snapchat generates the majority of its money in North America and Europe.

Indeed, Snapchat’s revenue per user in North America was $11.07 in Q3, up from $10.26 the previous quarter. By contrast, the platform only generated $1.13 per user in the Rest of World. That means that Snapchat is only seeing user growth in regions where it earns 90% less per user, which is based primarily on ad intake.

It's possible that Snapchat could also be hit harder than other apps by expanded teen social media bans, which are being considered or implemented in multiple markets. According to Pew Research published last year, around 55% of U.S. teens between ages 13 and 17 use Snapchat, making it the fourth most popular platform among this cohort, after YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

In Australia, which implemented social media usage restrictions for children under age 16 in December 2025, Snapchat said it subsequently locked or disabled more than 415,000 user accounts. These accounts, per Snapchat, had either been openly declared as belonging to a user under age 16, or Snapchat determined that was the case based on its age detection technology.

Snapchat said in August 2023 that it had more than 8 million users in Australia. That means the teen social media bans may have cost the platform around 5% of its total user base in that market.

Which may not seem like a major shift, but if Snapchat loses 5% of its users across the world, that would be significant, especially given its already shrinking growth margins. In addition, teen bans could also lead to Snapchat losing some of its value as the connection tool for younger audiences.

On the positive side, in his prepared remarks to accompny the earnings report, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said that average daily messages sent in the app increased 8% year over year in Q3, while the number of people engaging in two-way communication increased 6% year over year for the same period.

Spiegel also noted that the number of people posting to Spotlight grew 130% year over year, while daily active viewers increased 40% year over year, underlining the enduring value of short-form video content.

On the revenue side, the company's intake rose 14% year-over-year to $1.72 billion.

By region, overall third-quarter revenue in North America was up 13% year over year to $1.01 billion, while Europe was up 22 % to $363 million, and the Rest of World was up 11% to $345 million. Again, the revenue discrepancy between regions is notable here. Snapchat has three times more users in the Rest of World market versus EU, so while the revenue numbers between them are close, that doesn't equate to the same value, while it still generates the vast majority of its intake from the U.S.

Even so, the fact that Snap is seemingly succeeding in deriving more revenue from its key markets, despite no user growth, is also worthy of note.

In the accompanying earnings release, Spiegel said that artificial intelligence has become a significant advantage for the company’s teams and its ad platform.

Snap has also been working to evolve its business offerings, with improved creator partnership opportunities. The company also started pitching its ads to B2B brands.

Snap’s other big opportunity, per Spiegel, is its AR Specs, which launched in September. The $2,200 device is now available for pre-order in the U.S., France and the U.K., though it isn’t being shipped to users just yet.

Snap seems to hope the glasses will bring about new opportunities in advanced digital connection via wearable digital overlays.

But initial data in Snap’s own Q3 report showed that Specs sales haven’t contributed meaningfully to its bottom line yet. In a statement, Snap CFO Doug Hott said that advertising revenue grew 4% and the company’s “Other Revenue grew 84%,” led by Snapchat+, Memories Storage, and Lens+.

Overall, Snap’s third-quarter earnings data showed that the company still has a long way to go in securing its future prospects, and without any insight on the potential market for its AR Specs, it’s impossible to gauge consumer interest or the value of this element.

Subscription growth is relevant, but Snap appears to have a lot of other factors working against it that may impact its future results.

#7490. Agency execs call for retail media to be holistically considered beyond the lower funnel

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

As it continues to expand in the number of channels and options, as well as the ad revenue placed into it, retail media is offering media agencies new opportunities to harness closed-loop measurement in a way that benefits both upper- and lower-funnel marketing efforts.

That’s one major takeaway from a conversation onstage Dentsu’s president of commerce, North America, Aisha Khan, at Digiday’s Media Buying Summit last week in Newport Beach, Calif., last week. Khan said she also believes that the in-store side of retail media has great upward potential.

“There’s still tremendous growth to be had in the commerce landscape,” Khan told the audience, citing the stat that more than 80% of sales are still happening in store, but less than 5% of retail media is spent on in-store media. “So if you think about that expansion opportunity for retailers to really digitize the physical experience, that is going to create tremendous tremendous growth for retail media — think about that last point of purchase.”

In store may also be a way to bring down the expense of reaching consumers at the lower-end of the purchase funnel. “Retail media is very effective, right? It’s at one of the lowest points of in the funnel, and but it’s very expensive, so the efficiency is not quite there,” said Khan. “So I think in a good way there’ll be a bit more balance between the effectiveness and the efficiency, which will help to actually grow the next phase of commerce media, so I think while some areas will be will come down or plateau, there will be other areas of growth like the in-store piece.”

And in an earlier session on Day 2 of the Media Buying Summit, Instrument CEO Laurel Burton talked about how all the distraction around AEO and GEO has made the industry overlook the value of websites as part of an overall commerce strategy when, to her mind, the opposite is true.

“My prediction is the exact opposite that websites are dying,” Burton told the audience at a session on the melding of creative and tech with media. “I think they are the absolute central hub that needs to create a consistent experience because they’re feeding both that consumer and also that answer engine. You literally can’t be a product and a brand without this as a channel.”

Burton’s fellow speaker, Crocs CMO Carly Gomez (who happens to be an Instrument client), elaborated on Burton’s position saying the website needs to be coordinated in its messaging with other marketing channels.

“As people are discovering your brand, yes, they may come in through an LLM,” Gomez said. “But then if they want more information on your brand, their next stop either is your social media site or one of your social media handles or your e-commerce or your app. And essentially you want them all to feel cohesive and deliver the best possible experience.”

And yet, the upper-funnel brand-building side of retail media can’t be overlooked, argued Dentsu’s Khan, who pointed to the likes of CVS and Kroger as two retail media network providers who are helping to push the creative boundaries further (but didn’t elaborate).

“It goes back to ensuring that you’re getting the incrementality and the efficiency out of it, and that it’s worth the extra dollars that you’re paying for the closed-loop measurement,” she said. “People forget that there’s so much opportunity to come back to the power of creative in retail media, and I think retail media has been relegated to this performance marketing channel. But if you think about it, with the in-store and the shopper marketing experience, you still need that unmissable creative component too.”

Having just also picked up Diageo’s shopper marketing business, Khan noted that AI-powered Media Mix Modeling (MMM) will also help bring down the cost, even as consolidation will likely reduce the total number of retail media networks out there.

“Retail media’s boom was based on the back of closed loop measurement — this promise that you could understand with every dollar what you’re actually driving on the other side,” said Khan. “But I also believe AI has accelerated this idea of of agile MMM, or incrementality — more traditional MMM becoming more sophisticated. And so, as you think about closed-loop measurement, advertisers are investing in their own capabilities to invest across retailers and get that closed loop measurement themselves, instead of having the retailers grade their own homework. What happens is that data CPM that retailers have been charging for closed-loop measurement potentially does compress.”

#7489. Wendy’s takes a shot at McDonald’s with rewards-based video game

“WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones” challenges players to defeat enemies like the Golden Archers, and arrives as the chain chases a turnaround.

Wendy’s is continuing to target gaming communities with the launch of “WendyQuest,” its first fully-owned game. The standalone experience could help Wendy’s capture stronger engagement as the in-game advertising landscape grows saturated: Spending on in-game ads is expected to top $131 billion in 2026 and grow to over $217 billion by 2031.

“WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones” involves puzzles with turn-based battles, challenging players to go up against battle mechs, or oversized combat vehicles, including the Mech Chicken — a clear shot at rival McDonald’s. Players can power up with Jr. Bacon Cheeseburgers while navigating five food-focused regions, each of which offers a chance to earn Wendy’s food offers.

The effort offers up to 10 hours of gameplay and was built by hand over several years without the help of artificial intelligence shortcuts, according to the brand. Available prizes include a free medium fry, small frosty, 10 piece nuggets, biscuit or croissant or Dave’s Single. To redeem the reward, consumers need to copy a promo code from the inventory section of the game and enter it into the offers section of the Wendy’s app.

The launch of “WendyQuest” follows other gaming-focused efforts from the chain, including a tabletop role playing game in 2019 called “Feast of Legends,” which challenged players to fight against frozen beef. The chain also activated in Fortnite’s Food Fight game mode.

Other marketers have sought to appeal to gamers, from Panda Express to E.l.f. Cosmetics. Chili’s launched an online video game in 2024 digging at fast food restaurants that have jacked up prices. Gaming represents a valuable opportunity for brands looking to reach a wider audience: two-thirds of Americans between the ages of 5 and 90 game at least one hour per week, according to 2026 data from the Entertainment Software Association.

Wendy’s is currently in the midst of deploying a turnaround plan following ongoing challenges related to traffic and sales growth. The turnaround, which includes a focus on creating distinctive branding and marketing, is being led by Bob Wright, who has served as president and CEO since May. The chain in August brought on ex-McDonald’s CMO Tariq Hassan as chief marketing and customer growth officer. McDonald’s recently unveiled a new strategic plan that sees it shifting its approach to advertising and loyalty.

Wendy’s on Nov. 5 reported its third-quarter earnings, which include a 5.7% decrease in U.S. same-restaurant sales and a 2.2% increase in international same-restaurant sales, according to an earnings release.

#7487. Ad Tech Briefing: Google’s AI-reckoning

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →

It’s earnings season, typically the time of year when industry observers watch agog, as Big Tech companies post earnings far greater than the average ad tech company can begin to contemplate, but Q3 this year has thrown us a curveball to the usual narrative.

The unexpected glitch in the latest round ran contrary to the expected narrative, i.e., Google’s punishment for the success of its AI, a testament to the extent of the harsh realities facing the digital media sector as a whole when it comes to sustaining revenue.

It’s also likely to serve as an important footnote in the future filings of Google’s legal department, with tuned-in observers likely to recall how it was able to cite rapid AI advancements as proof of a fiercely competitive and evolving tech landscape.

Even if Google did lose both trials (on paper, at least) last year, it can be argued the above argument was made successfully to justify it continuing without forced divestiture, and in Q3 (it would appear) this argument impacted the biggest company in advertising’s bottom line.

Since then, Google has spent much of the year telling advertisers and investors that AI will make its search business bigger, not smaller. However, last week’s earnings offered the clearest indication yet that delivering on that promise is proving complicated.

On Oct. 28, Google’s parent company Alphabet reported that its search queries were growing at their fastest annual rate in five years, with total Q3 revenues nearing $127.6 billion, up 25% year-on-year.

However, a deeper analysis reveals a more troubling trend for the hegemon of Madison Avenue: more people are searching, but Google’s AI-driven search experiences aren’t yet generating ad revenue at the same rate as conventional search.

However, revenue from Google’s “Search & other” operations increased 12% to $63.35 billion, with Google’s chief business officer Philipp Schindler acknowledging as much during the company’s third-quarter earnings call, telling analysts that AI Mode’s comparatively limited monetization had contributed to the slowdown.

The disclosure is significant because search remains Google’s biggest financial engine and supports its (increasingly expensive) AI ambitions.

Advertising revenue, i.e., search in combination with other areas of its media operations, such as “YouTube” (Q3 revenues of $11.2 billion) and “Network” (Q3 revenues of $7.45 billion) — that’s the ad tech side, which is continuing its prolonged decline in revenue — accounts for approximately 64% of Alphabet’s revenue, down from 72% a year earlier.

More queries, less revenue per opportunity

Wall Street was unimpressed. Alphabet shares fell approximately 12.6% on Oct. 29, erasing close to $500 billion in market value, as investors questioned the economics of the company’s AI transition with coverage in the immediate aftermath of the results highlighting disappointment in Google’s revenue performance.

Google maintains that AI is expanding search activity rather than merely replacing existing queries. Sundar Pichai, CEO, Alphabet, told analysts that AI Mode queries are, on average, three times longer than traditional searches, while approximately one in five involves voice, images or documents.

However, executives also acknowledged that AI Mode currently monetizes at a lower rate, and further hinted that it is now expanding advertising within AI Mode internationally and introducing multi-turn advertisements in the U.S., allowing commercial placements to appear during extended conversations.

Meanwhile, the continued struggles of “Google Network” revenues, i.e., ad tech, is likely to stimulate further grimacing from publishers, with this unit generating a modest 1.4% gain in revenues during the period, with this trend accompanied by an overall increase in traffic acquisition costs, or “TAC,” of approximately 10% during the period.

Overall, TAC hit $16.4 billion, with the figures highlighting how higher impression prices can mask shrinking volumes as publishers contend with declining search referrals and unpredictable traffic. This creates an awkward backdrop for Google’s court-ordered ad tech remedies. Prebid’s proposed auction overhaul could improve publisher control and interoperability, but neither can restore lost audiences or guarantee advertiser demand.

“Can we really blame Apple for blocking ID tech?”

The platform wants to help advertisers align their promotions with users’ discovery behavior even as the company’s overall search traffic drops.

“Sociable” is the latest commentary on important social media developments and trends from industry expert Andrew Hutchinson of Social Media Today.

Reddit is testing ads in search results in the app, as the platform looks for more ways to help advertisers align with discovery behaviors.

As shown in these example screens, Reddit’s search ads will be targeted by query, and will include a small ad marker in the upper section of the panel.

As explained by Reddit: “People come to Reddit seeking human perspectives and experiences they can’t find elsewhere, with half of Reddit users saying the platform helps them discover something new. As we continue improving the user search experience on Reddit, we’re also beginning to test ad placements in search. These placements leverage existing ad targeting in search results pages on Reddit, which have high purchase and search intent.”

Reddit said the promotions will be shown in search results based on a range of factors, though these will primarily be aligned with contextual relevance.

Reddit has been working to improve its discovery tools as the app tries to help users find more relevant matches for their queries.

In July, Reddit published a study that found that 72% of its users come to the platform seeking information, and 64% of them have a specific goal in mind.

That also aligns with how Reddit gains traffic from search results, since the platform gets significant citation volume from AI chatbots.

However, AI traffic has started to dry up. Last week, as part of its Q3 performance update, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said that the company’s search traffic dropped by more than 1 million referrals per week on average in October.

That could reduce the value of its own in-app discovery process, though Tuesday’s announcement suggests that Reddit is clearly hoping to maintain its value as a product discovery tool.

Reddit said that it will initially test ads in search with a select group of eligible advertisers.
